assessment_summary: The statement incorrectly weakens the hypothesis of the Friendship Theorem (which requires every pair of vertices to have exactly one common neighbor) to "every edge lies in exactly one triangle". This modified condition is satisfied by any triangular cactus graph (where all cycles are triangles), such as a path of multiple triangles, or simply a disjoint union of triangles, none of which have a universal vertex.
counterexample:
Consider a graph consisting of three triangles arranged in a path (a triangular cactus). Let the vertices be {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} and the edges be the union of the edges of three triangles: {1,2,3}, {3,4,5}, and {5,6,7}. 

The 9 edges are {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3}, {3,4}, {3,5}, {4,5}, {5,6}, {5,7}, and {6,7}. The only triangles in this graph are the three listed above. Every edge in this graph lies in exactly one triangle.

However, the graph has 7 vertices and the maximum degree is 4 (for vertices 3 and 5). There is no vertex adjacent to all the others (a universal vertex would need degree 6). Therefore, it is not a friendship/windmill graph.

(Another trivial counterexample is the disjoint union of two separate triangles $K_3 \sqcup K_3$, which also satisfies the hypothesis but has no universal vertex).
